quotes.text: Patch Tuesday was never meant to be a deadline. It was a signal. Microsoft was telling you that new updates were available and that the clock had started.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes Patch Tuesday from a deployment date into the start of an exposure clock.

quotes.text: The cost of delay is invisible. Nothing happens until it does. And when it does, it's not a ticket. It's an incident.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why teams underestimate the risk of delaying updates.

quotes.text: Auto patch is a delegate, not an owner. You handed the work. You don't hand it the responsibility. So the right mental model is a contract with a clear split. Microsoft owns the mechanics. You own the outcome.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clarifies the responsibility split when using Windows Autopatch.

quotes.text: If you can't say which system owns a given setting, you already have a conflict. You just haven't seen it yet.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the one-owner-per-setting rule that prevents silent policy conflicts.

quotes.text: A left over group policy object is the most common silent blocker I know. It doesn't throw an error, it just keeps pointing the client somewhere else.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical troubleshooting insight from mixed management estates.

chapters.title: The old model and why it breaks
Desired state and Windows Update for Business
Update rings, deadlines and feature update policies
From patching devices to governing change

takeaways: Modern Windows updates run as a continuous, client-side system: Intune declares the policy and Windows Update for Business delivers, wherever the device is.
Design staged rings with real deadlines, pin feature versions deliberately against the support calendar, and use Autopatch to automate execution, not accountability.
Measure exposure windows and time to patch instead of a single compliance percentage, and give policy, pilots and exceptions named owners with a monthly review.
hook: Most teams still treat Windows patching as a monthly event, while updates now run continuously and exploits arrive within days. This episode walks IT admins through Windows Update for Business, Intune update rings, feature update policies, Windows Autopatch, expedited updates, drivers, reporting and troubleshooting. You will leave with an operating model that turns patching into governed, measurable change.
